title: Remote tactile sensing through optical fibers for robotics in extreme environments: a review
abstract: Abstract The advancement of intelligent robotic systems has driven increasing demand for tactile sensing technologies capable of reliable operation in extreme environmental conditions where conventional electronic sensors often fail due to electromagnetic interference, high temperatures, corrosive chemicals, or ionizing radiation. Optical fiber-based tactile sensors offer a promising alternative, combining electromagnetic immunity, high sensitivity, multiplexing capability, and mechanical resilience. These characteristics make them well suited for remote sensing tasks in challenging operational scenarios. Although several reviews have discussed optical fiber sensing technologies, limited attention has been given to their integrated application in tactile sensing for robotic systems operating under extreme environmental conditions, particularly with respect to emerging functional materials, harsh-environment adaptability, and next-generation intelligent robotic platforms. This review presents a comprehensive analysis of recent progress in optical fiber tactile sensing, focusing on robotics applications operating under extreme environmental conditions. We first outline the fundamental sensing mechanisms—namely, Fiber Bragg Grating (FBG), Fabry–Perot Interferometry (FPI), light intensity modulation, speckle pattern analysis, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and assess their performance in detecting force, pressure, temperature, and vibration. Subsequently, we examine advances in sensor materials, encompassing silica and polymer optical fibers (POFs), as well as emerging platforms based on hydrogels and micro/nanofibers (MNFs). Emphasis is placed on developments that enhance flexibility, stretchability, biocompatibility, and self-healing performance. These material innovations significantly expand the potential for deploying optical tactile sensors in dynamic and unstructured environments. The review further explores real-world applications where optical fiber tactile sensing has demonstrated impact, including minimally invasive surgical instruments, industrial automation systems, subsea exploration, extraterrestrial robotics, and disaster response operations. In each case, the ability to deliver accurate and high-resolution tactile feedback in harsh conditions is critical for safe and precise robotic manipulation. Emerging research directions are discussed, including the integration of artificial intelligence for tactile data processing, the development of bioinspired swarm robotic systems, and the implementation of self-adaptive and distributed sensing networks. Finally, we highlight critical challenges, such as signal drift, sensor miniaturization, packaging strategies, and long-term environmental stability, and propose future research pathways to support scalable, robust deployment. By providing a structured overview of current technologies, applications, and research challenges, this review aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers and engineers advancing high-performance tactile sensing in extreme robotic environments.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The rapid advancement of cyber-physical systems has catalyzed significant progress in intelligent service robotics, with recent systems demonstrating enhanced adaptability, real-time cognitive decision-making, multimodal perceptual integration, and sub-second response times [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. These capabilities have enabled intelligent robots to be deployed across diverse domains, including medical diagnostics and surgery [ 4 ,  5 – 6 ], industrial manufacturing [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ], and transportation and service sectors [ 10 ,  11 – 12 ]. A key area of innovation in this field lies in the development of biomimetic tactile sensing systems, which enable robots to perform dexterous manipulation and intelligent environmental interactions through real-time three-dimensional force mapping [ 13 ,  14 ]. These systems are inspired by the human skin’s dense neural network, which supports the perception of mechanical, thermal, and tactile stimuli. To replicate such functions, robotic tactile sensors are engineered to detect external cues, such as pressure, shape, temperature, and texture, while simultaneously providing feedback for adaptive control [ 15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 ]. To realize such intelligent sensing capabilities, recent research has focused on achieving broad detection ranges, high spatial resolution, rapid response times, and high accuracy. This has been accomplished through the integration of novel functional materials [ 19 ,  20 ], advanced 3D microstructural designs [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ], and sophisticated sensing mechanisms [ 24 ,  25 – 26 ]. In robotic tactile sensing, the term “extreme environment” generally refers to operational conditions characterized by high or low temperatures, elevated pressure, corrosive chemical exposure, intense electromagnetic interference, ionizing radiation, underwater or vacuum conditions, and mechanically hazardous or highly dynamic environments. These harsh conditions often exceed the operational limitations of conventional electronic sensing systems, motivating the development of more robust and interference-resistant tactile sensing technologies. Although numerous review articles have addressed flexible electronics, electronic skins, and general optical fiber sensing technologies, limited attention has been devoted to optical fiber-based tactile sensing systems specifically designed for robotic applications operating under such extreme environmental conditions. In particular, a systematic analysis integrating sensing mechanisms, advanced material platforms, harsh-environment adaptability, and multifunctional robotic applications remains lacking. Early efforts in robotic tactile sensing primarily emphasized mechanical optimization and actuator design. For instance, in a seminal study from 1986, researchers developed a three-fingered robotic gripper that incorporated rudimentary tactile functionalities, including force detection (0.1–10 lbs, with ± 0.01 lbs resolution), contact localization, and slip detection, although its performance was constrained by limited force resolution and bandwidth (< 5 Hz) [ 27 ]. Over the past two decades, breakthroughs in micro/nanomaterials [ 28 ,  29 – 30 ] [ 31 ], flexible electronics [ 32 ] [ 33 ,  34 ], and multifunctional tactile sensing architectures have significantly enhanced sensor performance [ 35 ,  36 – 37 ]. Materials such as graphene oxide (GO) [ 38 ,  39 ][[ 40 ], and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) [ 41 ,  42 – 43 ] have been introduced as highly flexible and sensitive sensing elements, exhibiting superior responsiveness and mechanical robustness compared to conventional metallic electrodes. Concurrently, sensor architectures have evolved from simple planar configurations to more complex three-dimensional geometries, including multilayered, porous, and array-based structures. For example, a templated laser-induced graphene (LIG) tactile sensor with a porous structure was developed [ 44 ], exhibiting high sensitivity (52,260.2 kPa⁻¹ in the 0–7 kPa range), rapid response/recovery times (12/46 ms), and an extended detection range (up to 1000 kPa). These innovations underscore how sensor functionality, particularly in terms of sensitivity, accuracy, dynamic range, and spatial resolution, can be significantly enhanced through judicious material and structural design, supporting applications in industrial automation [ 45 ,  46 – 47 ], healthcare [ 48 ,  49 ], robotics [ 50 ,  51 ], and intelligent transport systems [ 17 ,  52 ]. This review provides a comprehensive and focused analysis of optical fiber-based tactile sensing systems designed for robotic applications in extreme environments. We begin by discussing the fundamental operating principles of key optical fiber sensing mechanisms, including Fiber Bragg Grating (FBG), Fabry–Perot Interferometry (FPI), light intensity modulation, specklegram analysis, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR), evaluating their physical foundations, sensitivity, and robustness. We then examine recent advances in optical fiber materials, encompassing silica fibers, polymer optical fibers (POFs), hydrogel-based architectures, and micro/nanofibers (MNFs), with an emphasis on properties critical for harsh environments such as mechanical flexibility, stretchability, biocompatibility, and self-healing. Finally, we highlight emerging developments in hybrid optical tactile sensing platforms, which integrate multiple sensing modalities to simultaneously capture force, temperature, slip, and surface texture. By systematically synthesizing current research trends, challenges, and application opportunities, this review aims to guide the development of robust, high-resolution tactile sensing systems tailored for deployment in high-risk, dynamic, and unstructured environments.

sections.heading: Fundamentals of optical fiber-based sensing
paragraphs: Optical fiber-based sensing technologies operate on the principle that changes in environmental conditions can modulate specific properties of light, such as intensity, wavelength, phase, or polarization—as it propagates through or reflects within an optical fiber. These modulations arise from interactions between the guided light and external stimuli, enabling real-time monitoring of physical parameters such as strain, temperature, pressure, and vibration with high precision and sensitivity. Two primary mechanisms underpin the operation of most fiber-optic sensors. The first involves the inscription of periodic structures, such as fiber Bragg gratings (FBGs), within the core of the optical fiber. These gratings reflect specific wavelengths of light through Bragg diffraction, while allowing others to transmit. When external stimuli alter the grating’s periodicity or the refractive index of the fiber, the reflected wavelength shifts accordingly. This shift is directly correlated to the applied physical perturbation and can be measured with high accuracy using a spectrometer. The principles and performance of this sensing modality are detailed in Section II.A: Fiber Bragg Grating. The second mechanism involves direct geometrical or structural changes to the fiber itself, which affect how light is transmitted or scattered within the fiber. For instance, mechanical bending of the fiber can reduce light intensity or alter the spatial distribution of the light field. These perturbations can be analyzed through techniques such as Fabry–Perot Interferometry, light intensity modulation, and speckle pattern analysis, as discussed in subsequent subsections. To maintain a focused discussion relevant to robotic tactile sensing in extreme environments, this section emphasizes the fundamental sensing principles, operating mechanisms, and representative configurations of optical fiber-based sensors most applicable to high-resolution, robust, and interference-resistant tactile sensing systems. Detailed biomedical or chemical sensing examples are included only where they provide important insight into the sensing mechanism, material functionality, or structural design relevant to tactile sensing applications.

FBG sensors are highly sensitive, compact, immune to electromagnetic interference, and suitable for multiplexing via wavelength division. Temperature can have a significant influence on FBG sensor readings. In certain applications where the temperature variation is minimal, or the sensor is used solely for ambient monitoring, this effect may be negligible [ 55 ]. However, in environments with substantial thermal fluctuations, temperature-induced wavelength shifts must be compensated for to ensure accurate strain measurement. A widely adopted approach involves incorporating a temperature-compensating reference FBG outside the strain-sensitive zone. By assuming that this reference grating is isolated from mechanical strain, its response to temperature can be used to decouple thermal and mechanical effects in the primary sensing FBG [ 56 ,  57 ]. A fiber Bragg grating is essentially a periodic alteration of the core’s refractive index, formed by exposing the optical fiber core to spatially modulated ultraviolet (UV) laser light. Kawasaki et al. [ 58 ] first demonstrated the formation of refractive index modulation gratings in optical fibers. When light from an Argon-ion laser is launched into a short piece of optical fiber, interference between forward and backward propagating waves generates a periodic intensity pattern. Subsequent studies showed that when a UV interference pattern (∼244–248 nm) irradiates a photosensitive optical fiber, the refractive index of the fiber core undergoes permanent modulation. This creates a grating structure within the core, where a narrowband spectral component is reflected back when a broadband light source is launched into the fiber. The reflected wavelength, known as the Bragg wavelength (λ B ), shifts in response to external stimuli such as strain, pressure, or temperature, making FBGs ideal for highly sensitive and distributed tactile sensing applications. Any external disruption of the grating results in an equivalent change in the Bragg wavelength of the FBG sensor. The method of operation usually utilized in FBG sensor systems is to monitor this Bragg wavelength shift with regard to the perturbations corresponding to the measured (e.g., strain, temperature, or pressure). The interrogation technique is another name for this FBG sensor Bragg wavelength shift measuring technology. Only a few number of interrogation techniques have the potential to be developed into useful and affordable instrumentation systems for real-world applications, despite the fact that many different techniques have been proven in the literature. It is outside the purview of this review to go into great depth about these interrogation techniques. Additionally, several novel types of Bragg gratings, including chirped FBGs, apodized FBGs, phase-shifted FBGs, and superstructure FBGs, have been made possible by technical developments in fiber-grating production [ 59 ]. Because of their incredibly narrow reflection bandwidths (often less than 10 pm), which allow for high-resolution optical sensing, phase-shifted FBGs have garnered special attention among them. A prominent transmission peak in the reflection band is created by the redesigned grating structure’s introduction of a π phase shift in the periodic refractive index modulation. Because of this special characteristic, phase-shifted FBGs are ideal for accurate temperature, pressure, and strain monitoring in sophisticated tactile sensing applications.

Because of their simple structure, low-cost fabrication, and compatibility with basic photodetector-based readout units, intensity-modulated fiber sensors are widely used for strain, pressure, displacement, liquid-level measurement, refractive-index sensing, and environmental monitoring. Their immunity to electromagnetic interference, linear operating behavior, and suitability for remote and real-time measurements further underline their importance in the fundamental landscape of optical fiber-based sensing technologies. Another tactile sensing approach involves monitoring variations in transmitted optical intensity, which arise from bending-induced loss or structural deformation in the fiber. When an optical fiber is subjected to external forces, such as curvature, pressure, temperature, or strain—light transmission is affected due to bending losses and scattering. These variations can be captured by connecting a light-emitting diode (LED) or other illumination source to one end of the fiber and a photodetector to the opposite end. The basic mechanism involves mechanical deformation of the fiber, leading to asymmetric strain distributions that reduce the guided light intensity within the fiber core. Embedding the optical fiber in a soft, elastomeric matrix enhances sensitivity and durability by protecting the fiber and amplifying deformation responses. For example, researchers demonstrated an optical fiber-based tactile sensor integrated into robotic fingers, where local deformation was detected via intensity loss (Fig.  2 ) [ 66 ]. This setup enables feedback control for robotic manipulation tasks. An additional development involves the use of RGB-based sensing, wherein red, green, and blue light components are transmitted through the fiber. As the fiber bends or stretches, the spectral balance changes, altering the color output. A standard RGB camera can then detect these variations to infer tactile events. This method simplifies the system by eliminating the need for dedicated photodetectors or spectrometers. However, compared to wavelength- or phase-based sensing, intensity-based techniques are more susceptible to signal drift, ambient light fluctuations, and nonlinear response, requiring more advanced calibration or compensation algorithms. sections.heading: Output light specklegram
paragraphs: When coherent light propagates through a multimode optical fiber, a large number of guided modes with different phase velocities are excited. The interference between these modes produces a granular intensity pattern at the fiber output, commonly known as a specklegram. Each speckle corresponds to the superposition of modes traveling along different optical paths, each acquiring a distinct phase delay [ 68 ]. When the phase delay spans more than 2π, a well-defined interference pattern consisting of bright and dark spots becomes clearly observable at the fiber end. In addition to its fundamental physical behavior, the specklegram is extremely sensitive to external mechanical perturbations, making it suitable for tactile and deformation sensing. When coherent light propagates through an MMF, imperfections or microstructural variations modify modal interference, causing measurable changes in the speckle pattern. In speckle-based tactile sensors, changes in the spatial distribution or phase of the speckle pattern are used to infer the mechanical state of the fiber. For a given indentation depth or applied force, the response can vary depending on the hardness or mechanical impedance of the object in contact with the sensor. For instance, researchers developed a tactile sensing system based on specklegram analysis (Fig.  3 ), where variations in the interference pattern corresponded to different mechanical stimuli [ 69 ]. sections.heading: Surface plasmon resonance-based fiber-optic sensors (SPR)
paragraphs: Although SPR-based optical fiber sensors have been extensively explored for biomedical and chemical detection, the discussion presented here focuses primarily on the underlying plasmonic sensing mechanisms and their relevance to optical tactile sensing systems. Selected biomedical sensing examples are included to illustrate how SPR-enhanced fiber architectures, nanostructured plasmonic materials, and refractive-index modulation strategies can be adapted for highly sensitive tactile and environmental sensing platforms. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) refers to the resonant oscillation of free electrons at the interface between a metal and a dielectric, driven by incident light. SPR can be classified into two main types: planar SPR and localized SPR (LSP). The phenomenon of planar SPR was first observed in 1902 as spectral anomalies in light reflected from a metallic diffraction grating. Fano later attributed these effects to the excitation of surface electromagnetic waves on the grating surface [ 72 ]. Otto and subsequently Kretschmann and Raether refined the optical configuration required for SPR excitation. The Kretschmann–Raether configuration, which remains the basis for most modern SPR systems, involves a prism coated with a thin metal layer (typically silver, ~ 50 nm thick). When transverse magnetic (TM) polarized light impinges at a specific angle, surface plasmons are excited at the metal–dielectric interface, exhibiting evanescent decay into both media (Fig.  4 a). Where k 0  is the wavevector of the incident light in free space, and ε s , ε m  are the dielectric constants of the dielectric and metal, respectively. Because K sp  exceeds the propagation constant of incident light in the dielectric, additional momentum is required, typically provided via coupling schemes such as prisms, gratings, or waveguides, to excite the surface plasmons effectively. In contrast, localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) arises when incident light interacts with metal nanoparticles. The conduction electrons collectively oscillate, generating localized resonances at the nanoparticle surface (Fig.  4 b). Unlike planar SPR, where surface waves are delocalized along a continuous interface, LSPR is confined to sub-wavelength metallic structures and is highly sensitive to the surrounding refractive index, enabling ultra-sensitive optical fiber sensing platforms [ 76 ].

Localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) arises from the resonant interaction between incident electromagnetic waves and the collective oscillations of conduction electrons at the surface of metal nanoparticles. Upon excitation, the incident electric field displaces free electrons relative to the positive ion cores, generating a restoring Coulomb force that drives coherent electron oscillation (Fig.  4 b) [ 77 ]. This phenomenon leads to enhanced optical absorption at specific wavelengths, defined as the LSPR peak. The resonance conditions are highly sensitive to nanoparticle characteristics—including size, shape, composition, and to the dielectric environment. Changes in the surrounding refractive index alter the absorbed wavelength, which results in a shift of the LSPR peak observable in the absorption or transmission spectra. The readout process involved: (1) connecting an unpolarized light source to the fiber at one end using a microscope objective lens; and (2) gathering the light that was sent through the fiber from the other end using a spectrometer that was linked to a computer. After processing the transmitted spectra, the resonance wavelength at different glucose concentrations was found. A plasmonic fiber probe based on an epoxy layer and a nanohole gold sheet was reported for the detection of methanol [ 87 ]. To increase the sensor’s sensitivity, a MoS 2  layer was applied. The probe’s significant potential for real-world applications was proved when it was found to be insensitive for relative humidity in the range of 11–92%RH and remained constant for a year.

Siddharth et al. created an SPR-based probe to detect Escherichia coli (E. coli) for use in food and water quality monitoring [ 88 ]. A plasmonic fiber probe was recently created to detect breast cancer [ 89 ]. The probe was based on a silica fiber that was loaded with HER 2  antibodies and covered in a coating of gold. The concentration of the cancer biomarker was found to be as low as 10 ng mL − 1  (≤ 86 pM). In addition to glass and silica fibers, plastic fibers have also been utilized for SPR induction and sensing applications. For cortisol sensing applications, for example, a straight plastic optical fiber was coated with a gold/palladium alloy, functionalized with an anti-cortisol antibody, and passivated using bovine serum albumin. The probe was tested in different cortisol concentrations in the range of 0.005–10 ng mL − 1 . The resonant wavelength of the tested probe shifted15 nm for the tested concentration range and the limit of detection was 1 pg mL − 1 . The probe showed a sensitivity of 15-foldhigher than when it was functionalized with anti-hCG antibodiesthat showed 1 nm shift in the same cortisol concentration range. As the penetration of the evanescent waves and the interactionwith the dielectric analyte medium are the basis of the SPR-basedfiber sensors, it is essential to adequately expose the evanescentwaves to the analyte medium. Several optical fiber probe shapes, such as D-tube, tapered, and U-bent, have been proposed to increase the evanescent waves that reach the analyte medium [ 90 ]. For instance, a U-shaped fiber probe was created to detect glucose (Fig.  5 c). The glucose oxidase was immobilized over the gold nanoparticles that were affixed to the fiber core of the probe. When the glucose oxidase was oxidized in the presence of glucose solution, the film’s reflective index changed, which in turn caused a change in the gold nanoparticles’ resonant wavelengths’ absorption intensity (Fig.  5 d). The sensitivity of the fiber probe was significantly impacted by bending, and the greatest sensitivity was attained with a bending radius of 0.982 mm. The required blood sample was 150 µL, which is less than the 1.5 mL required by commercial sensors. In addition to enzymes like glucose oxidase and glucose peroxidase, selective glucose probes also rely on phenylboronic derivatives, which were developed for long-term glucose monitoring. For example, a self-assembled p-mercaptophenyl boronic acid (PMBA) was applied to a fiber coated with gold [ 91 ]. The PMBA monolayer placed on the gold layer changed its refractive index when cis-diol molecules like glucose interacted with it. Because glucose has a low molecular mass, the probe’s reaction to glucose fluctuation was negligible; as a result, no shift in the excited SPR wavelength was observed. To improve the probe’s sensing capabilities, gold nanoparticles modified with 2-aminoethanethiol (AET) and PMBA were added. The probe’s resonance frequencies showed a significant response to glucose concentration in the range of 0.01–30 m M and redshifted with changes in glucose concentration. With a limit of detection of 80 n M, the probe was extremely sensitive for glucose concentration. However, the long response time (12 min) and saturation time (53 min) both hindered the probe’s performance. A U-shaped plasmonic fiber probe coated with graphene for refractive index sensitivity was developed by Xie et al. [ 92 ]. When compared to the traditional gold-based straight plasmonic fiber, the combination of graphene and U-shaped design increased the sensitivity by almost five times. A monolayer of graphene was deposited atop the gold layer on the U-shaped fiber with a bent radius of 1.1 cm to produce a refractive index sensitivity of 15.52 μm RIU − 1 . A glass and polymer-based U-shaped plasmonic fiber probe was created by Manoharan et al. [ 93 ].

Before the gold nanostructures were grown, Ni/NiO was sputter-deposited on the U-region. With plasmonic peaks at 600 and 570 nm, respectively, the refractive index sensitivity for polymer and glass fiber probes was 27.66 and 25.65 ΔA/ΔRIU. A plasmonic fiberprobe was created by Divagar et al. to diagnose tuberculosis (TB) [ 94 ]. Gold nanoparticles functionalized with anti-M tb  LAM immunoglobulin M (IgG) were inserted into the U-bent fiber probe. M tb  LAM, a TB biomarker found in urine, was quantified by measuring the shift in light absorption with a fiber probe that was coupled to a green LED and a photodetector. It has been reported that a plasmonic plastic fiber may detect the chikungunya virus [ 95 ].The biomarker was the non-structural protein 3 (CHIKV-nsP 3 ). Gold nanoparticles were employed as labels on a U-shaped plastic fiber with a 0.5 mm core diameter. When a sandwich immunocomplex of CHIKV-nsP 3  was formed, the gold nanoparticles’ ability to absorb light changed. The probe had a limit of detection of 0.52 ng mL − 1  and a linear response in the range of 1–104 ng mL − 1 . Furthermore, the probes were more sensitive to CHIKV-nsP 3  compared to Pf-HRP 2 , HIgG, and the whole dengue virus. Because of their compact size, remote sensing capabilities, and capacity to examine minute samples, optical fiber-based SPR sensors have supplanted classic substrate-based SPR sensors. SPR-based fiber sensors are currently employed in many fields, including as life science, environmental safety, and biomedical diagnostics. Nevertheless, the signal-to-noise ratio restricts their resolution, sensitivity, and operating window. Additionally, the mode distribution at various incident angles is unstable and the propagating modes in multimode fibers are almost random. Additionally, the quality of the output signal is affected by the SPR-based multimode fiber sensors’ sensitivity to mechanical disturbances. On the other hand, a single-mode fiber-based SPR probe exhibits a narrow resonance dip in the transmission spectrum, leading to an increased detection limit. The single-mode fiber is therefore better. Thin films of graphene, molybdenum disulfide, molybdenum diselenide, tungsten disulfide, and tungsten diselenide are added to the plasmonic metal layer to improve the sensitivity and resolution of the SPR-based probes [ 96 ]. However, there are still issues including the requirement for expensive equipment and the complex, multi-stage fabrication process.

sections.heading: Tactile sensing based on optical fiber
paragraphs: In the context of robotic systems operating in extreme environments—including high or low temperatures, elevated pressure, strong electromagnetic interference, corrosive media, radiation exposure, underwater conditions, and mechanically hazardous settings—optical fiber-based tactile sensing platforms offer significant advantages over conventional electronic sensors. Their intrinsic immunity to electromagnetic interference, compact geometry, multiplexing capability, chemical stability, and remote sensing functionality make them highly suitable for deployment in harsh and dynamic operational environments. Accordingly, this section focuses on tactile sensing architectures and configurations that demonstrate enhanced robustness, environmental adaptability, mechanical resilience, and multi-parameter sensing performance under demanding operating conditions.

sections.heading: Fiber optic grating tactile sensors
paragraphs: Fiber optic grating-based tactile sensors utilize periodic refractive index modulations inscribed along the core of an optical fiber to detect mechanical deformations induced by external stimuli. Several types of gratings are used in these sensors, including long-period fiber gratings (LPFGs) [ 97 ], chirped fiber Bragg gratings (CFBGs) [ 98 ,  99 ], and uniform fiber Bragg gratings (FBGs) [ 56 ,  100 ,  101 ]. Among these, FBGs are the most widely adopted due to their relatively simple fabrication, compact size, high sensitivity, and cost-effectiveness.

sections.heading: Fiber Bragg grating tactile sensors
paragraphs: Although FBG technology has multiple advantages that make it a useful sensing tool in many different domains, it also faces certain particular difficulties. Multiple FBGs may be inscribed along a single fiber thanks to the technology’s high multiplexing capabilities. FBGs are particularly useful in settings with significant electromagnetic noise, such as power plants and substations, since, as previously indicated, they are resistant to EMI. FBGs’ adaptable design makes it possible to embed them into materials without changing their characteristics, which has major advantages for aeronautical and civil engineering [ 102 ]. This feature guarantees that variations in light sources or fiber loss have less of an impact on their performance, hence increasing measurement reliability over time.

FBG sensors are not without difficulties, even if their emphasis on wavelength shifts rather than intensity changes allows for reliable and precise observations. The high expense of interrogation devices, which are required to identify and examine the wavelength changes, is a major disadvantage. This may restrict the scalability of FBG systems, particularly in financially constrained applications [ 103 ]. Temperature cross-sensitivity is another problem; changes in temperature affect the Bragg wavelength and may cause problems for strain measurements. To precisely separate strain and temperature data, compensation techniques such the use of extra reference sensors are frequently needed. There are further difficulties with durability under challenging conditions. The necessity of efficient FBG sensor packing for offshore structure health monitoring is emphasized in [ 104 ], especially in floating, production, storage, and offloading units. To guarantee long-term sensor dependability, the best commercial packaging was chosen after extensive study and put to the test in challenging maritime environments including intense sunshine, torrential rain, and seawater. Furthermore, even though FBG sensors have multiplexing capabilities, the available wavelength range restricts how many sensors can be installed along a single fiber. To optimize the usefulness of sensors across a structure, this limitation requires careful design for sensor placement and spacing [ 105 ]. FBG-based tactile sensors function by monitoring shifts in the Bragg wavelength (λ B ), which occurs because of mechanical strain or pressure applied to the grating region. External forces induce elongation or compression of the fiber, altering the grating period and effective refractive index. This, in turn, shifts the reflected wavelength of light, which can be precisely tracked to quantify the applied mechanical load. A representative design—illustrated in Fig.  6 a and b—integrates an optical fiber into a hollow, rigid support structure capped with a soft elastomeric layer that transmits external pressure [ 106 ,  107 ]. For instance, researchers developed a helical embedding configuration, where the optical fiber is wound around the surface of a cylindrical substrate (Fig.  6 c and d) [ 55 ,  108 ]. This geometry reduces localized strain concentrations, mitigating the risk of fiber breakage while allowing controlled deformation of the fiber in response to external loads. These approaches demonstrate the versatility and adaptability of FBG-based tactile sensors, enabling reliable force sensing in dynamic environments while balancing sensitivity, mechanical resilience, and thermal stability. Fig. 6 Representative designs of fiber Bragg grating (FBG)-based tactile sensors. ( a ) Schematic of a tissue palpation sensor integrating FBGs into a flexible elastomeric layer for biomedical force detection. Adapted from Ref [ 106 ]. ( b ) Structure of a minimally invasive surgical force sensor utilizing dual FBGs, one for sensing and the other for temperature compensation. Adapted from Ref [ 107 ]. ( c ) Configuration of a soft surgical robotic platform employing helically embedded FBGs for distributed force sensing. Adapted from Ref [ 55 ]. ( d ) Spatial distribution of FBGs within a soft robotic manipulator, designed to enhance strain sensitivity while preserving mechanical compliance. Adapted from Ref [ 108 ]

To improve the durability and robustness of fiber-optic tactile sensors, structural innovations have been introduced that effectively mitigate strain concentration while preserving mechanical sensitivity. Researchers developed a modular tactile sensing array composed of five individual sensing units, each integrating a suspended optical fiber inscribed with FBGs, a contact interface, a helical elastomeric structure, and precision coupling components (Fig.  7 a) [ 109 ]. This modular architecture allows for scalable sensor assembly, where multiple units are interconnected via alignment slots and connection blocks to expand the detection range and spatial resolution [ 110 ]. Building upon this concept, researchers proposed a six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) force/moment (F/M) sensing system (Fig.  7 b), featuring a flexural body embedded with eight FBG-inscribed fibers at strategically selected positions [ 111 ]. This configuration enables the simultaneous detection of complex multi-axis forces and moments with high accuracy, essential for robotic applications requiring dexterous manipulation. Similarly, researchers introduced an FBG-based force and position sensor tailored for surgical forceps, capable of capturing deformation profiles in response to external loading [ 112 ]. These advances demonstrate the feasibility of high-resolution, multi-dimensional tactile sensing using FBG arrays, paving the way for enhanced robotic perception in constrained and dynamic environments. Fig. 7 ( a ) Schematic of a fiber-optic tactile sensor array consisting of five modular sensing units, each incorporating an FBG-inscribed suspended fiber, a helical elastomer, and structural connectors [ 109 ]. ( b ) Structural design of a six-axis force/moment (F/M) sensor incorporating eight strategically placed FBGs within a flexure body for multi-dimensional force detection [ 111 ]. ( c ) Schematic of a contact pressure sensor, in which a dual-FBG optical fiber is embedded using epoxy; one segment is encapsulated within a steel tube to isolate thermal effects [ 113 ]. ( d ) Tower-shaped sensing unit designed with fiber routing features and grooves for precise alignment, fabricated in a polyurethane elastomer matrix to ensure strain transmission and mechanical stability. For instance, researchers employed epoxy to secure a dual-FBG optical fiber within a composite structure, wherein one FBG was encased in a stainless steel capillary tube to serve as a thermal reference, enabling compensation for temperature-induced wavelength drift (Fig. 7c) [ 113 ]. In a parallel approach, a polyurethane elastomer-based tower structure was designed to guide and protect the optical fiber (Fig. 7d). The fiber was routed through designated grooves and supported along linear sections of each pillar, optimizing strain transfer and minimizing localized stress concentrations. These strategies collectively advance the mechanical reliability and long-term functional integrity of fiber-optic tactile sensing systems in complex environments

sections.heading: Tactile sensing based on optical fibers
Bragg grating-inspired fiber-based sensors
paragraphs: To overcome the intrinsic limitations of conventional FBG-based tactile sensors, several grating variants have been explored, among which chirped FBGs (CFBGs) and long-period fiber gratings (LPFGs) are the most representative. Variants of fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensors, such as chirped fiber Bragg gratings (CFBGs) and long-period fiber gratings (LPFGs), offer distinct operational advantages for tactile sensing applications [ 114 ]. CFBGs function as a cascade of FBGs with spatially varying grating periods, each segment reflecting a narrow spectral band. This distributed reflection enables higher sensing resolution and the capability to detect multiple physical parameters simultaneously. Real-time temperature sensing for medical thermal ablation in interventional cancer therapy is now the most developed and well-established use of CFBG sensors. Thermal ablation is widely used for electrical resections, pain management, and cardiac arrhythmia correction. However, in the last 20 years, it has become popular for the minimally invasive treatment of cancers, after they have been identified and targeted. High temperatures observed in the tumor tissue are the physical driver for thermal ablation, namely the thermal dose. Temperatures over 42–44 °C are hazardous for cells, according to Sapareto and Dewey [ 115 ]. Exposure to 52 °C for more than 60 s is a reference condition for clinical usage. The threshold for operation for fast ablation phenomena is 60 °C because the quick coagulation of proteins at this temperature ensures that the tumor cells in the tissue will die almost instantly [ 116 ,  117 ]. The objective of thermal ablation is to provide a highly selective thermal field to the tissue in a minimally invasive manner, exposing the whole tumor to ≥ 60 °C while preventing harm to healthy tissue. Electromagnetic principles are used in thermal ablation to provide energy to the tissue using a non-contact device or a percutaneous applicator with a small form factor and minimum invasiveness [ 118 ]. In radiofrequency ablation (RFA), a restricted heat field is applied to tissues with an impedance of 60–150 Ω using an RF generator operating at 450 kHz. A 2.4 GHz source connected to a miniature antenna is used in microwave ablation. A solid-state or fiber laser connected to a large-core fiber introduced into the tissue is used in laser ablation (LA) [ 119 ]. The sole non-contact ablation method is HIFU (High-intensity focused ultrasound), which uses an array to deliver focused ultrasound to a spot-size tissue.

Despite their high sensitivity and suitability for real-time temperature monitoring, CFBG sensors also face several inherent limitations that restrict their broader implementation in tactile and biomedical sensing applications. One of the main challenges is their temperature–strain cross-sensitivity, which can lead to inaccurate readings when both parameters vary simultaneously, requiring complex compensation or calibration techniques. Furthermore, the fabrication of chirped gratings demands precise control over the grating period and refractive index modulation, often involving costly and time-consuming inscription processes. This fabrication complexity limits large-scale production and sensor standardization. Another limitation is the spectral distortion or broadening of reflection peaks under non-uniform strain or temperature gradients, which can reduce sensing accuracy during dynamic operations such as tissue ablation or robotic manipulation. Additionally, while embedding CFBGs within flexible matrices such as PDMS enables multidirectional force mapping, it can introduce optical signal attenuation and mechanical drift due to polymer aging and thermal expansion. Lastly, the interrogation systems required for high-resolution wavelength tracking remain expensive and less portable, constraining the sensor’s integration into compact, low-cost robotic or medical devices [ 114 ]. For instance, by embedding orthogonally arranged CFBGs in a soft polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) matrix with staggered height configurations, researchers developed a two-dimensional tactile sensor capable of multidirectional force mapping (Fig.  8 (a)). Similarly, mounting CFBG arrays on rigid polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) substrates has been shown to improve both sensitivity and structural integrity (Fig.  8 (b)). In contrast, LPFGs produced through periodic refractive index modulation along the fiber core, manifest as attenuation bands in the transmission spectrum. These are highly suitable for applications requiring large-area, high-resolution monitoring due to their ability to couple light from guided modes into cladding modes over broad wavelength ranges. For example, LPFGs have been integrated into 3D-printed mechanical structures to assess localized strain distributions under tactile force (Fig.  8 (c)). Fig. 8 ( a ) Schematic illustration of a tactile force sensor integrating chirped fiber Bragg gratings embedded in a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) matrix, enabling multidirectional force perception through orthogonal grating alignment with spatial separation to avoid mutual interference [ 120 ]. ( b ) A polymer-based planar waveguide chirped Bragg grating (PPCBG) configuration designed to enhance spectral resolution and sensitivity for tactile sensing applications.( c ) Conceptual diagram of a long-period fiber grating (LPFG) subjected to external force, incorporated into a custom-designed, 3D-printed tactile structure for quantitative force assessment through strain-induced spectral attenuation [ 97 ]

sections.heading: Fabry–Perot interferometric tactile sensors
paragraphs: Fabry–Perot interferometric (FPI) fiber sensors offer exceptionally high sensitivity and precision for tactile and pressure sensing due to their ability to convert minute cavity length changes into measurable phase or wavelength shifts [ 121 ]. Their compact design and simple cavity structure enable versatile integration into various configurations, including intrinsic and extrinsic fiber geometries, allowing multiparameter detection such as temperature, strain, vibration, and acoustic pressure [ 122 ]. FPI sensors exhibit excellent performance under high-temperature conditions, with some designs operating up to 1,000 °C, making them suitable for harsh or extreme environments. They are also capable of detecting both static and dynamic mechanical stimuli, including vibrations, ultrasound, and acoustic waves, with high linearity and wide dynamic range. Furthermore, FPI-based sensors can achieve high spatial resolution and are compatible with MEMS and polymer diaphragms, enhancing their flexibility for robotic tactile sensing and biomedical applications [ 123 ].

Despite their superior sensitivity, FPI sensors present several challenges. The fabrication process requires high-precision alignment and cavity control, which increases complexity and cost compared with simpler fiber sensors. Cross-sensitivity between temperature and strain can lead to signal ambiguity, requiring complex calibration or compensation techniques to ensure measurement accuracy. The fragility of the cavity interfaces and potential degradation of reflectivity over time can reduce long-term reliability, particularly under high humidity or mechanical vibration [ 124 ]. In addition, signal demodulation and phase-tracking electronics are relatively expensive and sensitive to optical noise, which complicates multiplexing in large-scale sensor networks. Finally, while FPI sensors excel in laboratory and controlled-environment tests, maintaining performance stability in field-deployed tactile sensing systems—such as robotics operating in dynamic or high-temperature conditions—remains an ongoing challenge [ 125 ]. Fabry–Perot interferometer (FPI)-based tactile sensors rely on microcavities formed between the fiber tip and a reflective surface. External pressure alters the cavity length or refractive index, thereby shifting the interference pattern. This optical phase modulation is highly sensitive to mechanical stimuli such as contact force, vibration, or displacement. A typical design employs a hemispherical reflective nozzle that modifies the optical path based on the surface roughness and force applied (Fig.  9 ). In dual-cavity configurations, one cavity is dedicated to force sensing while the other compensates for temperature fluctuations, ensuring improved measurement fidelity. Further enhancements involve cascaded FPI structures that integrate air and silica cavities to simultaneously decode both force and temperature parameters through decoupled signal analysis. These designs are especially valuable in minimally invasive surgical applications and other domains where compact, multi-parameter sensing is essential [ 126 ]. Fig. 9 Structural schematic of a tactile sensor based on Fabry–Perot interferometry (FPI), featuring a hemispherical probe tip and an internal cavity configuration for high-sensitivity force detection. External pressure induces micro-scale displacements in the reflective diaphragm, resulting in optical path length variations that shift the interference spectrum. Adapted from Mo et al. [ 127 ]

sections.heading: Optical transmission-based tactile sensors
paragraphs: Despite these limitations, optical transmission-based tactile sensors have been successfully designed in various configurations, enabling robust, real-time, and multidimensional force sensing. Optical transmission–based tactile sensors obtain tactile information by analyzing changes in the transmitted or output light within the sensing medium. These sensors typically employ optical fibers or waveguides as light-transmission paths, meaning that the inherent advantages of optical fibers—such as lightweight, mechanical flexibility, chemical inertness, fast response, and compact size—translate directly into benefits for tactile sensing applications. In addition, optical transmission–based sensors are immune to electromagnetic interference (EMI), enabling their integration with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems and minimally invasive surgical (MIS) tools [ 16 ]. When configured as array-type sensors, optical transmission–based systems also avoid electrical interconnections between individual sensing points, thereby eliminating parasitic disturbances common in capacitive and piezoelectric tactile sensors. The primary sensing mechanisms in these devices rely on light intensity modulation, fiber Bragg grating (FBG) technology, and interferometric detection, with the first two being most widely applied in current tactile sensing research.

However, despite these significant advantages, optical transmission–based tactile sensors also present several limitations that restrict their broader implementation. The fabrication and assembly of optical components often require high-precision alignment and specialized equipment, which increases overall production cost and complexity. Moreover, the optical signal can be easily affected by variations in the light source intensity, fiber bending, or coupling losses, leading to measurement instability under dynamic or highly deformable conditions. The interpretation of optical signals, particularly those involving intensity modulation or interferometric detection, also demands complex demodulation algorithms and calibration procedures, which may limit their practicality in real-time or large-scale tactile sensing systems. Furthermore, optical fibers are inherently fragile and can suffer from microbending or mechanical breakage under repeated stress or impact, reducing the long-term durability of the sensor in harsh or high-contact environments.  These limitations highlight the need for continued material innovation and improved packaging strategies to enhance the robustness and reliability of optical transmission–based tactile sensing systems in real-world applications.  Unlike FBG- or FPI-based systems, optical transmission-based tactile sensors detect external stimuli by monitoring light intensity variations within a deformable optical path. These sensors forego complex grating structures, instead relying on mechanical modulation of the light path through bending, strain, or refractive changes. In a bioinspired design, optical microfiber couplers embedded in PDMS emulate the mechanoreceptive function of human skin. As deformation alters coupling efficiency, distinct spectral changes in output light correspond to mechanical input (Fig.  10 (a)). Another approach embeds fibers in soft hydrogels such as agarose, capturing stress-induced changes through dynamic speckle pattern analysis (Fig.  10 (b)). To enhance linearity and robustness, novel geometric structures have been explored. For instance, thermoplastic urethane substrates with triangular profiles induce controlled fiber bending under load, enabling predictable light modulation (Fig.  10 (c)). Alternatively, integrating RGB light sources into silicone matrices allows for color-resolved tactile detection, where variations in transmitted light spectra signify deformation (Fig.  10 (d)). This technique reduces system complexity while maintaining reliable force detection, making it well suited for soft robotics and wearable systems [ 128 ]. Fig. 10 ( a ) Schematic illustration of the biomimetic optical skin (BOS), incorporating an optical microfiber coupler neuron (OMCN) embedded in a flexible PDMS matrix for multidimensional haptic sensing [ 129 ]. ( b ) Optical fiber embedded in an agarose matrix for speckle-based tactile sensing, enabling detection of external stress via speckle pattern modulation [ 69 ]. ( c ) Side-view diagram of a deformation-induced optical transmission tactile sensor, utilizing thermoplastic urethane (TPU) with a triangular profile to enhance fiber-bending response under pressure. ( d ) Color-coded tactile sensor integrated with RGB LEDs within a soft silicone substrate, enabling light component differentiation through mechanical deformation [ 39 ]

sections.heading: Tactile sensors using silica fiber
paragraphs: Silica-based optical fibers have become integral in the development of tactile sensors due to their low optical loss, high mechanical strength, and compatibility with various sensing architectures. These fibers are widely employed in sensing strain, pressure, vibration, acceleration, temperature, and humidity, in addition to their established role in optical communications. Among the most commonly used configurations for fiber-based sensing are the fiber Mach–Zehnder interferometer (FMZI), Fabry–Perot interferometer (FPI), and fiber Bragg gratings (FBG). Of these, FBGs have garnered significant attention owing to their compactness, wavelength-encoded responses, and integration with subwavelength or nano-engineered periodic structures within the fiber core. For example, researchers developed a multi-parameter probe by embedding dual FBGs in a PDMS film, enabling simultaneous measurement of heart rate, respiration rate, and body temperature [ 130 ]. They also introduced a wearable glove module containing five FBGs embedded along each finger, with accompanying algorithms to resolve joint bending angles with an average error of 0.47 ± 2.51° (Fig.  11 a) [ 131 ]. Furthermore, they enhanced the stretchability and sensitivity of FBG sensors by pre-configuring the optical fiber in a sinusoidal layout within an elastic substrate, achieving a sevenfold sensitivity improvement compared to traditional straight embedding [ 132 ]. In addition to FBGs, FPI-based structures offer advantages in wearable sensing due to their simplicity, compact form factor, and high sensitivity. Researchers demonstrated a strain sensor based on an in-fiber air cavity Fabry–Pérot interferometer (FPI) [ 133 ], and further streamlined the fabrication process by inserting photopolymerizable polymers between two single-mode fibers to form an FPI cavity (Fig.  11 b(i)). Similarly, they implemented an FPI-based chest strap capable of detecting respiration and heart rate with a measurement error below 5% (Fig.  11 b(ii)) [ 134 ]. FMZI sensors are also effective in tactile applications. These sensors consist of a sensing arm, a reference arm, and two fiber couplers. Incident light is split and travels through both arms before recombining, and variations in external stimuli lead to differential phase shifts. The resulting interference fringe pattern reflects changes in pressure or vibration. embedded FMZI-based sensors within silicone elastomers to mimic human skin’s ability to perceive complex mechanical stimuli such as vibration, sliding, and tapping [ 135 ]. Wang et al. developed a health-monitoring mattress incorporating an FMZI sensor between two elastic layers (Fig.  11 c), capable of detecting micro-pressures from respiration and heartbeats. Phase modulation in the output signal allowed real-time derivation of respiratory frequency, amplitude, heart rate, and cardiac signal strength. Compared to FBGs, FMZI sensors benefit from simplified fabrication and do not require high-cost equipment, making them highly suitable for scalable and wearable tactile sensing platforms. (i) Positional shift of FBG nodes corresponding to metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint angles. (ii) Structural layout of the wearable hand module. (iii) Comparison of measured and actual joint angles [ 132 ]. ( B ) Low-power portable Fabry–Perot interferometer (FPI) system for physiological monitoring. (i) Schematic and photographic view of a Fabry–Perot cavity-based sensing structure. (ii) Remote sensing schematic utilizing an energy-efficient portable interrogator. (iii) Illustration of a smart textile integrated with an FPI sensor for simultaneous heart rate and respiratory monitoring. Inset shows the representative FPI spectrum captured by the interrogator [ 134 ]. ( C ) Optical fiber Mach–Zehnder interferometer (OF-MZI)–based mattress for vital sign detection. (i) Schematic of the OF-MZI structure. (ii )  Conceptual diagram for capturing respiratory and cardiac signals via pressure-induced phase modulation. (iii) Representative signals acquired by the mattress for respiration and heartbeat monitoring [ 136 ]

Tactile sensors employing silica-based optical fibers offer several compelling advantages for remote tactile sensing applications. Because silica fibers are electrically insulating, they provide intrinsic immunity to electromagnetic interference (EMI) and can safely operate in high-voltage or MRI environments — a major benefit for robotics and biomedical settings. Their small diameter and lightweight construction allow for integration into compact, flexible tactile arrays or embedded robotic end-effectors, and their chemical inertness and high thermal tolerance make them suitable for harsh or extreme-environment deployment. Moreover, silica fibers enable remote sensing via long optical runs and multiplexing along a single fiber, reducing wiring bulk and enabling distributed sensor networks [ 137 ]. However, these benefits are tempered by several key limitations. The cost and complexity of high-precision interrogation equipment and fiber handling are higher than many traditional sensors, constraining scalability. Silica fibers are also relatively brittle compared to polymer alternatives, making them vulnerable to micro-bending losses, breakage under mechanical stress, or degradation in dynamic tactile contact environments. The signal fidelity can degrade due to bending losses or optical coupling issues, which complicate calibration and reduce robustness over time in robotic tactile skins [ 138 ]. Furthermore, while silica fibers support high temperature use, they are often paired with coatings and buffer materials that may limit flexibility or degrade under repeated tactile loading, appearing less ideal for conformable large-area tactile surfaces

sections.heading: Polymer-based tactile sensors using optical fiber
paragraphs: Polymer optical fiber (POF)-based tactile sensing systems have attracted growing interest for robotic applications operating in dynamic and extreme environments due to their flexibility, lightweight nature, mechanical compliance, and resistance to electromagnetic interference. Compared with rigid silica fibers, POFs provide improved deformability and impact tolerance, which are advantageous in environments involving repetitive mechanical stress, large deformation, underwater operation, or human–robot interaction. Therefore, this section emphasizes recent developments in POF-based tactile sensing platforms that enhance environmental adaptability, stretchability, thermal response, and operational robustness for next-generation robotic systems. Polymer optical fibers (POFs) have emerged as a promising alternative to conventional rigid silica fibers, particularly in the domains of short-range communication and tactile sensing. Their inherent softness and mechanical tunability allow for intimate conformability to complex surfaces, making them well suited for wearable and flexible sensor platforms. By adjusting the chemical composition of the core and cladding materials, key mechanical parameters such as elasticity and tensile strength can be precisely controlled. Moreover, the relatively large core diameters of POFs (typically in the millimeter range) facilitate efficient coupling with light sources and detectors, further supporting their integration into compact, low-power optical systems [ 139 ].

sections.heading: Fundamentals of POF-based tactile sensing
paragraphs: Structurally, POFs comprise a high-refractive-index core surrounded by a lower-refractive-index cladding, enabling light propagation via total internal reflection. In contrast to electrical signals, optical signals offer multidimensional information channels intensity, wavelength, polarization, and phase that can be harnessed simultaneously for tactile perception. Among these, intensity and wavelength are the most frequently exploited for direct measurements in tactile sensing. Under external mechanical perturbations such as bending or stretching, light leakage increases due to changes in the internal reflection condition, resulting in transmission losses. Monitoring the output light intensity thus enables the quantification of tactile inputs. Additionally, functional integration with wavelength-sensitive materials, such as fluorescent dyes, nanoparticles, or Bragg gratings, enables wavelength modulation for enhanced sensitivity and parameter selectivity. Despite their advantages, many commercially available POFs (typically based on polycarbonate or PMMA) are limited by high Young’s modulus, which restricts their flexibility and strain sensitivity. To address this limitation, emerging high-performance POFs are being engineered using softer, highly elastic polymers that can be fabricated at scale, significantly enhancing their applicability in next-generation tactile sensing [ 140 ].

sections.heading: POF-based tactile sensor architectures
paragraphs: POF-based tactile sensors leverage the inherent flexibility, tensile resilience, and lightweight nature of polymeric fibers, enabling high sensitivity to strain, pressure, and temperature. Although several examples discussed in this section originate from wearable or biomedical sensing studies, they are included because the underlying sensing mechanisms, soft-material integration strategies, and structural designs are directly transferable to robotic tactile sensing systems operating in complex or extreme environments. In particular, concepts such as stretchable fiber architectures, multi-parameter sensing, soft mechanical compliance, and distributed deformation monitoring provide important design insights for robotic grippers, underwater manipulators, flexible electronic skins, and human–robot interaction platforms requiring robust tactile perception under dynamic operating conditions. Furthermore, functionalization with nanoparticles (gold or upconversion particles) or fluorescent dyes allows multi-parameter sensing, wavelength modulation, and decoupling of strain and temperature signals. Their softness, biocompatibility, and electrical safety make them ideal for wearable health monitoring, gesture recognition, and robotic tactile applications. Recent developments have leveraged diverse materials and structural configurations to advance the capabilities of POF-based tactile sensors across multiple sensing modalities, including strain, pressure, and temperature. The inherent flexibility and tensile resilience of polymeric materials make POFs especially well-suited for strain sensing. For instance, a dye-doped PDMS fiber demonstrated stable and linear optical response across a dynamic strain range up to 100%, enabling real-time detection of human activities such as vocalization and finger motion. A separate design employed two silica fibers within a liquid-filled polymer tube to realize a tactile sensor with high angular resolution (0.18°) and a low detection limit (0.7 mN), highlighting the potential of hybrid fiber structures for precise touch sensing. To further enhance sensitivity, gold nanoparticles (GNPs) have been embedded within POFs, yielding a pressure sensitivity of 3.05 dB/N (Fig.  12 A), significantly amplifying the optical response to mechanical stimuli. In addition to mechanical sensing, thermal sensitivity is another essential parameter. By integrating thermally responsive upconversion nanoparticles, tactile sensors with detection limits as low as ± 0.3 °C have been achieved, enabling reliable temperature monitoring across a broad operational range (25–70 °C). More recently, multi-parameter sensing capabilities have been demonstrated through the incorporation of temperature-sensitive fluorescent nanoparticles into the POF core. By decoupling strain and temperature signals through simultaneous tracking of excitation and emission intensities at multiple wavelengths, these advanced fiber-based sensors achieve a high level of functionality and adaptability essential for next-generation tactile systems [ 141 ]. Fig. 12 Polymer Optical Fiber (POF)-Based Tactile Sensors. ( A ) A highly sensitive tactile sensor integrated with gold nanoparticles (GNPs). (i) Schematic representation of the sensor structure. (ii) Time-resolved response of the sensor under incrementally applied loads ranging from 0 to 6 N [ 142 ]. ( B ) A stretchable POF-based temperature sensor demonstrating enhanced thermal sensitivity and mechanical flexibility [ 141 ]. ( C ) A frictional sensing unit based on an optical fiber knot, enabling detection of lateral tactile interactions. ( D ) A strain sensor constructed from thermoplastic elastomers for real-time monitoring of body movement.  (i)  Illustration of the sensor’s mechanical architecture and its stretchable design. (ii) Application example showing a wearable knee brace integrated with the sensor for continuous tracking of knee flexion angles during walking and running [ 143 ]. ( E ) A gesture recognition glove embedded with distributed POF-based tactile sensors. (i) Optical image of the distributed POF network. (ii) Photograph of the glove worn for capturing hand gesture inputs [ 144 ]

The POF-based temperature sensor shown in Fig.  12 B demonstrated high sensitivity (1.3%/°C) with a linear response, even under 40% strain, making it well-suited for stretchable wearable systems. Detecting both vertical and lateral forces is vital in tasks requiring precise manipulation. To enable multi-axis decoupling, researchers developed an anisotropic waveguide tactile sensor capable of sensing normal and shear forces with sensitivities of 28 mN and 81.1 mN, respectively [ 145 ]. Similarly, the frictional sensing strategy depicted in Fig.  12 C, inspired by knot mechanics, utilized a deformed fiber topology to achieve sensitivities of 2.67 N⁻¹ (normal) and 5.59 N⁻¹ (frictional). Due to their softness and electrical safety, POFs are ideal for wearable health monitoring. A textile-integrated POF sensor has been developed for real-time heart and respiratory rate monitoring, with minimal errors of 2 breaths per minute and 4 beats per minute. For large-motion detection such as limb movement, strain sensors with high mechanical resilience are essential. As shown in Fig.  12 D, a co-extruded thermoplastic elastomer-based strain sensor maintains stability under strains exceeding 300% and is used to track knee flexion during locomotion. Gesture recognition was demonstrated using a glove equipped with distributed POF sensors (Fig.  12 E), capable of detecting individual finger joint angles [ 144 ]. To enhance robotic functionality, soft prosthetic hands and grippers have incorporated POF-based strain sensors. For instance, researchers employed lithographically patterned POFs integrated with photodiodes and LEDs to enable tactile discrimination of object shape and softness [ 146 ]. They further advanced underwater robotic manipulation using a soft POF-integrated gripper combined with machine learning for real-time contact localization (Fig.  12 F) [ 147 ]. Despite these advances, challenges remain such as thermal instability, viscoelastic drift, and cross-sensitivity among sensing parameters. Emerging high-performance designs (anisotropic waveguides, co-extruded thermoplastic elastomers, textile-integrated networks) address some of these limitations, advancing POF-based sensors toward robust, remote tactile sensing applications.

sections.heading: Hydrogel-integrated fiber tactile sensors
paragraphs: To provide a more analytical perspective, Sects.  5 –8 compare the operational principles, material characteristics, sensing performance, and environmental adaptability of different optical fiber–based tactile sensing technologies. Particular emphasis is placed on sensitivity, mechanical robustness, thermal stability, multiplexing capability, fabrication complexity, and suitability for robotic operation in extreme environments.  The following sections therefore synthesize the advantages ,  limitations ,  and application potential of hydrogel-integrated fibers ,  micro/nanofiber systems ,  and advanced robotic sensing architectures rather than presenting only descriptive summaries of individual studies.  Hydrogels have emerged as promising platforms for wearable, implantable, and robotic tactile sensors due to their tissue-like softness, high water content, and biocompatibility. Recent efforts have explored their integration into fiber architectures. Stretchable hydrogel fibers made from alginate–polyacrylamide blends exhibit high mechanical resilience and optical stability under repeated strains up to ~ 700%. Spatially distributed sensing was achieved by incorporating dye-doped regions along the fiber (Fig.  13 A). To address water sensitivity and limited stretchability, Chen et al. developed GN-fibers with an elastic modulus of 32.6 MPa and low optical attenuation (0.26%/cm), enabling multifunctional sensing of strain, pressure, and bending (Fig.  13 B). However, hydrogel fibers are prone to dehydration and mechanical failure. Addressing this, Bai et al. introduced self-healing polyurethane-urea optical fibers. These demonstrated rapid self-repair and real-time feedback control in soft quadruped robots, enabling autonomous adaptation after damage (Fig.  13 C). Novel strategies improving molecular mobility and reversible bonding have yielded self-healing optical fibers with propagation losses as low as 0.31 dB/cm and broad thermal stability (–77 to 168 °C) [ 148 ]. Despite these advances, hydrogel fibers remain prone to dehydration and mechanical failure under prolonged use, and ensuring long-term environmental stability and mechanical robustness continues to be a challenge. Achieving high-performance designs often requires complex fabrication techniques, such as reversible bonding or minimizing optical propagation loss. sections.heading: Micro/Nanofiber-based tactile sensors
paragraphs: Driven by the need for high-resolution, miniaturized sensing, optical micro/nanofibers (MNFs) have gained attention for tactile applications. With diameters near or below the wavelength of visible and NIR light, MNFs offer ultrahigh flexibility, low optical loss, and tunable geometry. Fabricated via taper drawing, MNFs can guide light with significant evanescent fields due to high index contrast with substrates such as PDMS. The unique characteristics of MNFs tight light confinement, enhanced sensitivity, and spatial resolution make them highly suitable for rapid, low-power tactile sensing. Their compatibility with multifunctional, skin-like interfaces positions MNFs as a next-generation platform for intelligent wearable and robotic systems [ 152 ].

The miniaturization of optical tactile sensors has advanced significantly through the development of micro/nanofibers (MNFs), offering high sensitivity, fast response, and superior spatial resolution due to their subwavelength dimensions and large evanescent fields. By monitoring force-induced variations in transmitted light intensity and relative humidity, integrated hierarchically structured sensors can differentiate finger proximity from direct touch (Fig.  15 B, iv–v). Despite their ultrahigh sensitivity and spatial resolution, MNF-based tactile sensors suffer from limited mechanical robustness due to their subwavelength diameters, making them vulnerable to breakage during fabrication and repeated deformation. Precise alignment and encapsulation within elastomeric matrices increase fabrication complexity and restrict large-area scalability.
