sections.heading: Strengths and weaknesses of current studies
paragraphs: Recent advances in optical fiber–based tactile sensing have significantly expanded the possibilities for robotic interaction in extreme environments. The studies reviewed in this work demonstrate remarkable progress across multiple sensing platforms—silica fiber sensors, polymer-based optical fibers, hydrogel-integrated fibers, and micro/nanofiber architectures. Despite these achievements, current research still faces several scientific and technological limitations that hinder large-scale deployment. The following section provides a consolidated analysis of the strengths and weaknesses observed across the current body of literature. A key strength of existing studies is the high sensitivity and precision achieved by modern optical transduction mechanisms. Fiber Bragg gratings (FBGs), Fabry–Perot interferometry (FPI), speckle-based sensing, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) all exhibit exceptional strain, pressure, and vibration sensing resolution, enabling fine tactile perception far beyond the capabilities of traditional electronic sensors. Another core advantage is the intrinsic immunity to electromagnetic interference (EMI), which allows reliable operation in high-voltage, high frequency, or radiation-rich environments where electronic tactile sensors typically fail. This characteristic is particularly advantageous for robotic systems in nuclear facilities, deep-subsea structures, and aerospace applications.

Current studies also highlight the mechanical adaptability and versatility of material platforms. Polymer optical fibers (POFs) provide superior flexibility and large elastic deformation ranges, enabling integration within soft robotic structures, wearable devices, and bioinspired systems. Hydrogels, with their tunable mechanical properties and biocompatibility, support tactile sensing in biomedical tools and delicate manipulation tasks. Furthermore, micro/nanofiber sensors exhibit ultralight weight, extreme compliance, and high surface-area-to-volume ratios, allowing unprecedented sensitivity to weak forces and subtle surface interactions. Another strength is the progress in distributed and multiplexed tactile sensing. Many studies demonstrate the ability to integrate multiple sensing points along a single optical fiber using wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM), time-division multiplexing (TDM), or spatial multiplexing. This enables high-density tactile mapping suitable for robotic skins, grippers, and navigation systems operating under complex conditions. Collectively, these innovations underline the strong research momentum and the growing maturity of the field.

Despite these advancements, several limitations remain prevalent across current studies. One of the primary weaknesses is cross-sensitivity, particularly between strain, pressure, and temperature. Many optical fiber tactile sensors require complex calibration or dual-parameter compensation to distinguish overlapping stimuli, which becomes especially challenging in extreme environments with rapidly changing conditions. In addition, signal drift and long-term instability are frequently reported, especially for hydrogel-based and polymer-based systems that are prone to swelling, dehydration, creep, or photodegradation. Mechanical durability remains another concern. Although POFs and hydrogels offer excellent flexibility, they often suffer from low mechanical fatigue resistance under repeated loading, bending, or torsion cycles. Micro/nanofiber tactile sensors, while highly sensitive, tend to be fragile and difficult to package for harsh environments such as high-pressure ocean depths or high-temperature industrial settings. Silica-fiber-based sensors, in contrast, are mechanically robust but exhibit limited stretchability, restricting their use in soft robotics and deformable interfaces. Technologically, current studies are limited by the complexity and cost of interrogation units, especially for interferometric and SPR-based systems requiring high-precision optical alignment or specialized demodulation algorithms. This complexity reduces portability and hinders adoption outside laboratory environments. Another significant weakness is limited real-world validation. Many studies demonstrate performance only under controlled laboratory conditions, with scarce data on field deployment, multi-parameter disturbances, long-term cycling, or environmental aging. Furthermore, there is a lack of standardized benchmarking protocols, making direct comparison between studies difficult.

sections.heading: Applications in extreme-environment robotics
paragraphs: The deployment of robotics in hazardous environments, such as industrial manufacturing, disaster response, and defense is increasingly essential due to escalating safety and efficiency demands. In such settings, robots can replace human labor to perform high-risk tasks. Two main approaches exist: the use of a highly capable single robot or a distributed system composed of simpler units. While a multifunctional robot may offer strong performance, it is often expensive and less flexible. Alternatively, swarm robotic systems, inspired by biological collectives, offer robustness, scalability, and cost-efficiency [ 161 ]. Swarm robotics is a paradigm in which a large number of simple robots cooperate to perform complex tasks through local interaction and decentralized control, emulating behaviors seen in ants, bees, birds, and fish. Key advantages of swarm systems include Scalability: Performance can improve with the addition of agents; Robustness: Failure of individual robots has limited impact on system-level performance; Adaptability: Functions can be reconfigured by adding or removing robot types.

Despite these strengths, several challenges remain cumulative error due to scale, difficulties in coordination through only local communications, and the increased complexity of real-world applications. Among the most relevant bio-inspired tasks in harsh settings is exploration, where swarm robots may offer superior reliability over single-agent systems, especially in chemically or radiologically contaminated environments. Heterogeneous swarm architectures, comprising robots with varied sensing or actuation capabilities, enable specialized task delegation, such as source localization followed by remediation. However, increasing swarm capability also elevates system cost, making optimization of swarm size a key research focus [ 162 ].

sections.heading: Swarm robotics
paragraphs: Swarm robotics operates under three core principles: Large robot populations; Tasks that are difficult or inefficient for single robots; Local communication only. The two defining features are decentralized control, where each robot operates autonomously without central oversight, and self-organization, a collective behavior that emerges from local rules. A classical biological example is ant foraging: ants leave pheromone trails that attract others, leading to efficient path optimization through positive feedback. These systems exhibit: Dynamism; Emergence of global order; Negative feedback for stabilization; Multistability due to stochastic decision-making. Such biological analogues have laid the foundation for scalable and resilient swarm control architectures [ 163 ].

sections.heading: Bio-inspired Swarm systems
paragraphs: Nature-inspired control strategies are central to swarm robotics. Common behaviors include Aggregation: Fundamental for group formation; flocking: Coordinated movement akin to bird flight; Exploration and foraging: Environmental mapping and resource identification; Collective transport: Load sharing by multiple agents. Aggregation is particularly significant, with mechanisms classified as: Cue-based, where environmental factors like light or temperature guide clustering; Self-organized, where interactions alone produce coherent patterns. The integration of both strategies enhances system adaptability in unpredictable environments [ 164 ].

sections.heading: Biological foundations
paragraphs: Exploration is a ubiquitous behavior in social insects. Ants, bees, and caterpillars must locate and evaluate food sources under resource and energy constraints. These evolved behaviors, shaped by millions of years of natural selection, demonstrate efficient strategies for dynamic environment assessment, which are readily translatable to robotic systems.

sections.heading: Robotic implementations
paragraphs: Numerous studies have validated swarm-based exploration. For instance, collaborative vs. non-collaborative robot teams show that cooperation improves infrared target localization. Subsequent works have incorporated odor-based navigation and reinforcement learning to improve adaptability. Performance in large-scale environments has been shown to improve with swarm size and communication range. Key contributions include: Swarm control for landmine detection and firefighting [ 165 ]; Environmental mapping using low-cost mobile swarms [ 162 ]; Optimization methods to reduce computational complexity [ 166 ]; High-volume exploration using 100 robots for unknown terrain mapping [ 167 ]. A notable example is the introduction of a heterogeneous swarm combining Foot-Bot (ground mobility), Hand-Bot (manipulation), and Eye-Bot (aerial surveillance) [ 168 ]. This division of labor displays the power of functional diversity in addressing complex, real-world missions.

sections.heading: Strengths and weaknesses of applications and future directions
paragraphs: Optical fiber–based tactile sensing technologies have been deployed across a diverse range of robotics applications operating in extreme environments, including minimally invasive surgical systems, soft robotic manipulators, subsea inspection platforms, planetary exploration rovers, industrial automation in hazardous zones, and disaster-response robotics. The reviewed studies collectively demonstrate the considerable potential of optical tactile sensors to enhance robotic capability in environments where traditional electronic sensors are limited. Nonetheless, these applications reveal several practical constraints that must be addressed for broader adoption. This section synthesizes the major strengths and weaknesses observed across these application domains.

A major application-level strength is the reliability of optical tactile sensors in environments characterized by high electromagnetic interference (EMI). Their intrinsic EMI immunity enables stable sensing in medical operating rooms with electrosurgical instruments, industrial settings with high-power motors, and subsea environments where communication signals may be disrupted. This reliability ensures consistent tactile feedback during mission-critical robotic operations. In minimally invasive surgery, optical fibers’ small diameter and biocompatibility allow seamless integration into surgical needles, catheters, and end-effectors, enabling high-resolution force detection that enhances procedural accuracy and patient safety. Another strength is the superior environmental resilience of optical fiber systems. Silica-based sensors exhibit outstanding resistance to heat, corrosion, hydrostatic pressure, and ionizing radiation, making them particularly suitable for subsea exploration, high-temperature industrial inspections, nuclear waste handling, and extraterrestrial missions. Polymer optical fibers and hydrogel-integrated sensors contribute further advantages such as flexibility, mechanical compliance, and adaptability to soft robotic skins and wearable systems. These characteristics facilitate safe human–robot interaction, deformable grippers, and distributed tactile sensing across non-planar surfaces. Applications also benefit from the long-distance sensing capability of optical fibers, which allows remote operation in dangerous or inaccessible environments. In disaster-response and planetary robotics, signals can be transmitted over kilometers with minimal loss, enabling human operators to receive high-fidelity tactile information while remaining shielded from hazards. Additionally, advances in multiplexing enable large-area tactile mapping, supporting robotic navigation, manipulation, and surface characterization in complex terrains.

Despite their advantages, application-level weaknesses remain significant. One of the major issues is integration complexity, especially in systems that require bending, twisting, or large deformations. Soft robotics presents particular challenges, as embedding optical fibers without degrading sensitivity or damaging the fiber under dynamic motion is difficult. Packaging strategies often add stiffness to the system, reducing the compliance needed for soft manipulation tasks. Another weakness is the susceptibility to cross-parameter interference, especially in applications where temperature, pressure, and mechanical strain vary simultaneously. For example, in subsea robotics, depth-induced pressure and thermal gradients can distort force measurements unless advanced compensation methods are implemented. Similarly, in surgical applications, body temperature fluctuations and fluid interactions can affect sensor output, demanding robust calibration techniques. Mechanical durability and reliability also pose challenges across several domains. Hydrogel-based and polymer-based tactile sensors may degrade under prolonged contact with biological fluids, seawater, or industrial chemicals. Micro/nanofiber-based devices, while highly sensitive, remain fragile and difficult to encapsulate for rugged field deployment. In extraterrestrial environments, extreme thermal cycling and radiation exposure can induce microcracks or attenuation changes in the fiber, reducing long-term reliability. Another limitation is the lack of standardized testing protocols across applications. Studies often employ different force ranges, environmental conditions, interrogation systems, and performance metrics, making cross-application comparison difficult. This inconsistency reduces engineering confidence for real-world deployment. Furthermore, real-time data processing challenges remain in high-speed applications such as robotic manipulation, where complex optical signals (speckle patterns, interferometric phases) require computationally intensive algorithms that may not be feasible for lightweight robotic platforms. Overall, the applications of optical fiber-based tactile sensors demonstrate strong promise for enabling robust, high-resolution force feedback in environments that challenge traditional sensing technologies. Their immunity to electromagnetic noise, environmental resilience, and compatibility with long-distance communication provide clear advantages across biomedical, industrial, subsea, and extraterrestrial robotics. However, practical integration barriers, cross-sensitivity issues, durability constraints, and a lack of standardized evaluation methods continue to limit widespread adoption. Addressing these challenges through improved packaging, advanced signal processing, and unified testing frameworks will be critical for translating laboratory-scale demonstrations into operational robotic systems capable of consistent performance in extreme environments. In light of the identified strengths and application-level limitations, future research on optical fiber–based tactile sensing should focus on translating demonstrated laboratory capabilities into robust, deployable robotic systems. Addressing integration complexity will require the development of advanced packaging and embedding strategies that preserve fiber sensitivity while maintaining mechanical compliance, particularly for soft robotics and deformable interfaces. To mitigate cross-parameter interference in real-world environments, future systems should incorporate multi-parameter decoupling approaches through hybrid sensor designs, material engineering, and intelligent signal processing frameworks. Enhancing mechanical durability under prolonged exposure to biological fluids, seawater, radiation, and thermal cycling will be critical for long-term deployment in surgical, subsea, and extraterrestrial applications. In parallel, simplifying interrogation architectures and reducing computational overhead will be essential to enable real-time tactile feedback on lightweight and mobile robotic platforms. Finally, establishing standardized testing protocols, application-specific benchmarking metrics, and large-scale field validations will be vital for objectively assessing performance across domains and accelerating the adoption of optical fiber–based tactile sensors in operational extreme-environment robotics.

sections.heading: Conclusion and outlook
paragraphs: The integration of optical fiber–based tactile sensors into robotic systems has substantially advanced remote tactile perception, particularly for operation in extreme environments. Compared with conventional electronic sensors, optical fiber–based approaches offer intrinsic immunity to electromagnetic interference (EMI), high sensitivity, multiplexing capability, long-distance signal transmission, and robust performance under harsh conditions such as high temperature, radiation, corrosion, and pressure. These advantages make optical fibers a foundational technology for reliable tactile sensing in next-generation robotic platforms. This review has systematically summarized recent progress in optical fiber–based tactile sensing, with a focus on sensing fundamentals, material platforms, and application-driven design strategies. Core sensing mechanisms—including fiber Bragg gratings (FBGs and CFBGs), Fabry–Perot interferometers (FPIs), and optical transmission–based methods—enable precise detection of strain, pressure, temperature, vibration, and dynamic contact. Material innovations ranging from rigid silica fibers to polymer optical fibers, hydrogels, self-healing elastomers, and micro/nanofibers have expanded the mechanical compliance, biocompatibility, and functional versatility of tactile sensors. These developments have enabled diverse applications in minimally invasive surgery, wearable healthcare, soft robotics, subsea exploration, nuclear facilities, planetary exploration, and disaster-response robotics, where accurate and robust tactile feedback is critical. Despite significant advances, several challenges continue to limit large-scale deployment beyond laboratory demonstrations. These include signal drift and cross-sensitivity in multi-parameter environments, mechanical fragility under repeated deformation, constraints on miniaturization and integration, long-term material degradation, and the high cost and complexity of optical interrogation systems. Addressing these limitations is essential for translating optical fiber–based tactile sensing into reliable, field-deployable robotic technologies. To provide a more focused and application-oriented outlook, the future research directions discussed in this section emphasize specific technological and engineering challenges associated with extreme-environment robotic operation. Particular attention is given to AI-assisted signal interpretation, self-healing sensing materials, multi-parameter decoupling strategies, scalable photonic integration, radiation-resistant packaging, and distributed tactile intelligence for autonomous robotic systems. In addition to highlighting emerging opportunities, the discussion also considers practical barriers including fabrication scalability, computational complexity, environmental reliability, and long-term operational stability under harsh working conditions.

Looking forward, the evolution of optical fiber–based tactile sensing for extreme-environment robotics is expected to be shaped by several key research directions. First, artificial intelligence–enhanced tactile processing, including machine learning and multimodal data fusion, will play a central role in interpreting complex optical signals and enabling real-time adaptive control. Second, self-healing and self-calibrating sensing platforms, enabled by dynamic polymers, embedded feedback mechanisms, and adaptive compensation algorithms, will improve durability and operational longevity. Third, further miniaturization and system-level integration—through soft lithography, photonic integration, and scalable sensor arrays—will support high spatial resolution while maintaining mechanical flexibility. Fourth, bioinspired and swarm robotic systems incorporating distributed tactile intelligence may enable collective perception and autonomous interaction in unstructured environments. Fifth, enhanced environmental resilience, achieved through radiation-hardened materials, advanced encapsulation strategies, and robust packaging, will be critical for extreme-condition deployment. Finally, standardization and scalable manufacturing processes will be essential to facilitate commercialization, interoperability, and cost-effective adoption across robotic platforms. While these future directions present strong opportunities, their practical realization will require careful consideration of engineering constraints, fabrication complexity, long-term reliability, and data availability—particularly for AI-driven approaches operating under extreme conditions. Interdisciplinary collaboration among materials science, photonics, robotics, and artificial intelligence will be vital to overcoming these barriers.

In summary, optical fiber–based tactile sensors are poised to become a core component of intelligent robotic systems, enabling human-like dexterity, adaptive decision-making, and autonomous operation in environments beyond the reach of conventional sensing technologies. Continued innovation and realistic system-level validation will ultimately define their impact in expanding the operational boundaries of extreme-environment robotics.
